item.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
The Riemann Hypothesis
#

Every nontrivial zero of the zeta function has real part 1/2. That limits the error in the prime count. The claim is still unsolved.

Prime numbers do not sit at a regular spacing. The count of primes up to a large number does follow a smooth trend. The Riemann hypothesis is a precise claim about how far that count can stray from the trend.

Bernhard Riemann stated it in 1859. On November 24, 2026, it is still open. It is one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. The Clay Mathematics Institute offers US$1 million for a proof or a disproof that meets its rules. Clay Mathematics Institute

The path through the idea is short. §1 defines primes. §2 counts them. §4 hides that count inside an infinite product. §8 states the claim. §9 says what the claim would control.

item.title: Kinds of Numbers: A Map from Natural to Complex
item.author: hari@dasarpai.com (Dr. Hari Thapliyaal)
item.description:
Kinds of Numbers
#

Nested sets from counting to the complex plane, plus bases and computer formats
#

Natural → integer → rational → real → complex is the main ladder. Each step adds numbers the previous step could not hold.

Rows marked ladder nest: each set keeps every number from the smaller set and adds more. An irrational number is a real number with no exact fraction, such as $\sqrt{2}$. An imaginary number is a real multiple of $i$, such as $3i$, inside $\mathbb{C}$.

Kind Symbol (usual) Lives in One-line idea Example
Natural $\mathbb{N}$ ladder Counting sizes $1, 2, 3, \ldots$
Whole $\mathbb{W}$ ladder Natural plus zero $0, 1, 2, \ldots$
Integer $\mathbb{Z}$ ladder Whole numbers and negatives $-3, 0, 7$
Rational $\mathbb{Q}$ ladder Ratio of two integers $\tfrac{3}{4}$, $-2$, $0.125$
Real $\mathbb{R}$ ladder Rationals plus irrationals (e.g. $\sqrt{2}$, $\pi$) $-1.5$, $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\pi$
Irrational — $\mathbb{R}$, not $\mathbb{Q}$ No exact fraction form $\sqrt{2}$, $\pi$
Imaginary — inside $\mathbb{C}$ Real multiple of $i$. The number $3i$ sits on the imaginary axis. The number $0 = 0i$ is the origin, on the real axis and on the imaginary axis. $3i$, $-i$
Complex $\mathbb{C}$ ladder Real part plus imaginary part $2 + 3i$

Two phrases sound alike but mean different things:

  • Kinds of numbers — which set a value belongs to ($\mathbb{Q}$, $\mathbb{R}$, …).
  • Positional number system — how you write a value in a base (decimal, binary, hex).

This article maps the sets first, then points at bases and floating-point formats data work uses every day.

For symbols and operators used with these numbers, see Grammar of Mathematics: Operators, Functions, Relations, and Symbols.
